newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia plans convention to consider republic.
newsitem.headline: Australia plans convention to consider republic.

text.p: Australia will hold a 10-day convention in December to consider whether the country should become a republic, replacing Britain's Queen Elizabeth as head of state, Prime Minister John Howard said on Wednesday.
But Howard, an avowed monarchist, emphasised that his government had no particular commitment to the republic, a favourite cause of former Labor prime minister Paul Keating.

"The commitment to hold the convention does not represent any decision by the government that a change is necessary or desirable, nor any dissatisfaction with the workings of the current system," Howard told parliament.
The Labor opposition, defeated in elections by Howard's conservatives a year ago, has ridiculed the government's plans for a constitutional convention as an attempt to bury the issue.
Faced with pressure for change, Labor says, Howard chose to set up a committee -- hardly a decisive move.
But Howard himself said the convention would stick to the issue of the republic, and not wander into the distractions of other constitutional issues.

"(The government) has decided that on balance this convention should deal only with the question of the head-of-state and therefore any possible change to a republican form of government," Howard told parliament.
The republican cause has lost momentum since Howard replaced Keating as prime minister in the March 1996 elections.

Opinion polls show that about half of Australians favour a republic but also that they think the country has more pressing problems. Many people do not care whether the British monarch or an Australian president is head of state.
As soon as Keating left, the official rhetoric vanished and public discussion of the republic subsided.
Howard said the convention would have 152 delegates and public input would be encouraged.
"Public submissions will be invited to allow the community to inject into the convention ideas on these issues," he said.
The government will appoint half of the delegates and the remainder will be chosen by a voluntary public vote.
Voting in Australia is usually compulsory.
The appointed delegates would comprise 40 parliamentary delegates -- 20 from state and territory parliaments and 20 from federal parliament.
The other appointed delegates would include Aboriginal groups, local government and young people.

The British monarch is titular head of state of Australia, which is a member of the Commonwealth of former British colonies. The monarch is represented in Australia by the governor general, whose role is largely ceremonial.
Republicans argue that Australia's retention of the British monarch as head of state is highly anachronistic.
Monarchists say that a change would have no substantial advantage and might even destablise the political system by creating a president with real power backed by popular vote.
